title: trace-latency-decomposition-audit
content:
Purpose:
This is an investigative working note summarizing end-to-end latency traces collected from the production serving runtime over the last two weeks (2026-02-22 -> 2026-03-08). Goal: identify dominant contributors to tail latency (p95/p99), actionable mitigations, and a prioritized experiment plan. This doc collects span-level breakdowns, representative traces, hypotheses, and quick wins.

Data sources and instrumentation: 
- Distributed tracing (internal trace ids) with per-span timestamps for: ingress, auth/validation, routing, queueing, batching, GPU scheduling, KV cache lookup, model kernel execution (split where available into attention, MLP, softmax kernels), GPU->CPU copy, detokenize/postprocess, and response streaming.
- Aggregated request meta: model variant, request length (input tokens), requested max_new_tokens, tenant tier (hosted/free vs dedicated), and route config.
- Sampling: 10% continuous trace sampling + targeted full-trace capture for requests taking >2x median.
- Infra metrics: GPU utilization, host CPU steal/irq, memory pressure, NVLink errors, node-level checkpointing jobs.

Summary (aggregate numbers across captured window):
- p50 E2E latency: 84 ms
- p95 E2E latency: 340 ms
- p99 E2E latency: 1,420 ms
- Median payload size: 32 tokens input, 64 tokens generated (typical chat flow)
- High-variance cohort: requests with input >128 tokens or max_new_tokens >256 account for 18% of traffic but 56% of p99s.

Per-stage median/p95/p99 breakdown (representative buckets, numbers in ms):
- Network ingress + LB hop: p50 5 / p95 12 / p99 30
- Auth/validation + request decode: p50 2 / p95 8 / p99 25
- Routing & policy eval: p50 3 / p95 10 / p99 40
- Queueing (pre-batching): p50 6 / p95 65 / p99 500
- Batching wait time: p50 8 / p95 120 / p99 750
- Tokenization + encoding: p50 1.5 / p95 6 / p99 20
- KV-cache lookup (embedding/prefix cache): p50 4 / p95 20 / p99 200
- Model forward / GPU kernels (total): p50 40 / p95 90 / p99 260
  - attention kernels (subset): p50 18 / p95 42 / p99 110
  - MLP kernels: p50 15 / p95 30 / p99 80
- GPU->CPU copy + postprocess: p50 5 / p95 20 / p99 75
- Response streaming flush: p50 1 / p95 12 / p99 40

Observed patterns and root-cause hypotheses:
1) Queueing & batching long-tail is the largest single contributor to p99 (combined ~60–70% of tail time):
   - Long input/generation-length requests wait significantly longer before the batch triggers (adaptive batch timeout currently 8 ms with max_batch_size 16); when long-token requests arrive they block batch throughput and increase wait time for subsequent requests.
   - Multi-tenant noisy neighbors: certain tenants with large max_new_tokens settings produce sporadic large batches that saturate single GPU slots and push other requests into long queueing windows.

2) KV-cache misses and cold-cache warming spikes add substantial latency for some requests:
   - p99 traces show repeated 60–200 ms stalls aligned with first request to a model variant after deployment or after cache eviction.
   - Misses correlate with infrequent model variants and low reuse routes (usually lower-tier customers on hosted).

3) Kernel variance on long sequences: attention kernel time increases non-linearly with sequence length; p99 dominated by requests with long context (>=1024 tokens). When long sequences combine with higher batch sizes, contention on GEMM/attention kernels increases tail.

4) Background IO / maintenance tasks on certain nodes cause sporadic p99 spikes:
   - Node-level traces show GPU stalls aligned with host checkpointing/backup cronjobs that kick in at 03:00 UTC on subset of clusters.

5) Copying and serialization overheads: repeated copies when fallback to CPU-resident logits occur (rare) add tens to hundreds of ms in tail cases.

Representative trace snippets (redacted ids):
- trace 2026-03-06-XY12 (p99): total 1,720 ms -> queueing 520 ms, batching 620 ms, model kernels 300 ms, kv-cache lookup 180 ms. Input tokens 512, max_new_tokens 512. Tenant: hosted-free.
- trace 2026-02-28-AF03 (p99): total 1,380 ms -> queueing 420 ms (burst of 7 concurrent long jobs), background node IO 210 ms (momentary GPU stall), kernel tail 340 ms.

Quick wins (priority order):
- Reduce batch-trigger latency for requests with small token counts when queue contains older requests, by implementing per-request age-based priority (fast-path for interactive). Goal: cut p95 queueing by 20–40% for interactive cohort.
- Add per-tenant soft limits on max_new_tokens and surface warnings in console for hosted free tier to avoid unbounded long-job injections.
- Increase KV-cache TTLs for common prompts / enable proactive warming for high variance routes (synth requests to warm cache on model rollout).
- Introduce async GPU->network flush path to avoid synchronous copy penalties for streaming responses (low-risk refactor).

Medium-term experiments (A/B):
- Adaptive batching policy: implement size-and-age hybrid trigger (if oldest request > X ms then flush, else wait up to Y ms or until N requests). Experiment matrix: X={12,20}, Y={4,8,12}, N={8,16}. Track p50/p95/p99 and request-level fairness (head-of-line latency).
- Dynamic model-variant routing: route long-generation requests to dedicated reserved pools (or slower, cheaper quantized variants) to isolate noisy jobs. A/B: route 25% of long jobs to dedicated pool.
- Kernel fusion & fused attention experiment: run microbenchmarks on fused kernels for sequence lengths 512/1024 to measure p99 improvements.

Observability & follow-ups:
- Create a dashboard showing: per-route p50/p95/p99 with stage breakdown (queueing, batching, kernel, postprocess) and 7-day trend. Alert if p99 increases >30% vs baseline.
- Add sampling metadata to traces: include node-level cron schedule and GPU maintenance label so we can correlate spikes to infra events.
- Export a curated set of 200 p99 traces to bucket storage and attach to the tickets for deeper per-layer profiling (nvprof/cuda-trace).

Risks & open questions:
- Changing adaptive-batch thresholds may increase server throughput cost; need cost vs latency tradeoff analysis.
- Proactive warming increases request overhead and memory pressure on KV-cache. Determine eviction policy impact.
- Dedicated routing for long jobs requires capacity commitments and may hurt unit economics; start with small pilot on spot/dedicated reserved nodes.

Action items (owners):
- (Maya) Implement per-request age-based fast-path prototype and test under canary traffic (due 2026-03-24).
- (Arjun) Add KV-cache warm-on-deploy hook + TTL tuning experiment for two heavy routes (due 2026-03-18).
- (Lena) Build dashboard (Grafana) with stage breakdown panels and p99 alert (due 2026-03-17).
- (Noah) Run fused-kernel microbenchmarks and collect NVLink/GPU utilization correlation (due 2026-03-31).

Notes to reviewers: this doc is a working investigation. Data extracts are noisy — I intentionally left raw representative traces for reproducibility. Please add observed traces or counterexamples in comments. If you have infra logs that align with the 03:00 UTC spikes, add them to ENG-1284.

References: linked artifacts above (PR/issue) and model perf benchmarks in internal repo.

End of note.
